content.p: Peter Clarence Foster has spent four decades in and out of courtrooms on three continents. His convictions include fraud, false advertising, money laundering, contempt of court, assaulting police and entering a country without a visa. Courts in Australia, Britain, the United States and Vanuatu have sentenced him. He has served time in several of those countries, and more than once he has fled before a sentence could be carried out.

For most of that time his business was the same: products sold on promises that were not true, above all slimming aids. His name reached a wider audience in 2002, when he was reported to have helped the wife of the British prime minister buy two flats. In 2020 he was arrested on a beach in Queensland, and in 2025 he was still in court there on fraud charges, which he denies. A person charged is not a person convicted, and this account keeps the two apart.
content.h2: Insurance, tea and the first fines
content.p: The Guardian traced Foster's criminal record to 1983, when he was fined at the age of 20 after trying to defraud an insurance company. The paper gave the fine as GBP 75,000 and the sum claimed as GBP 40,000. The Independent said the fine was 40,000, over a claim on a cancelled flight, and The Age put the attempted claim at GBP 40,000. The outlets therefore differ on what the penalty was. They agree that he was in his early twenties and that the offence was the start of a long record.

The Independent described him as a boxing promoter in his teens who was later bankrupted when he did not pay the advertising bills for a Muhammad Ali bout that was never held. The Guardian said he was declared bankrupt in Australia a year after the insurance case, after trying to market a "magic" method of giving up smoking.

The product that made his name was Bai Lin tea, sold in Britain in the 1980s as an "ancient Chinese diet secret". The Age wrote that the idea of slimming tea was introduced to him by Muhammad Ali's wife and that he first tried it in Australia, which drew the attention of the competition regulator there. The British model Samantha Fox, then his girlfriend, promoted it. The Guardian reported that when the tea was tested it turned out to be ordinary black China tea, and that his company was fined GBP 5,000 for breaching the Trade Descriptions Act. Fox later told the Mirror that she was 22 and impressionable at the time and would never be taken in again.

Foster left Britain in 1988 and escaped prosecution then, according to the Independent. In the United States the tea was renamed. The Age said it was sold as Chow Low Tea with newspaper advertisements claiming it lowered cholesterol whatever the user ate, and The Guardian spelled the name Cho Lo. He was convicted and served four months in a Los Angeles jail, ABC News reported, for conspiracy to commit grand theft according to The Guardian. The Age added that he also cleared rubbish from freeways, and that on his release he began marketing a jelly called Ageless Aging.
content.h2: Prison in Britain and flight to Australia
content.p: Foster returned to Britain in 1994. The Independent said a court fined him GBP 21,000 that year for trade description offences over the tea; The Age said the fine was for the Bai Lin scam. The following year, Liverpool Crown Court convicted him of a conspiracy involving slimming granules that broke trading standards regulations. The Guardian said he was jailed for two years after persuading a former slimmer of the year to say falsely that she had lost 12 stone. The Age said he was also facing prosecution over his role as a director of a company called Foremost Body Corporation.

While on day release from prison he travelled to Australia on a false passport. The Guardian placed his arrest at Darwin airport in October 1996. The Age wrote that the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission was waiting for him and that he was fined A$15,000 over a "thigh contour treatment" called Biometrics, with an undertaking not to make further claims about its effects. Britain still wanted him. He was arrested under extradition proceedings, was given bail, absconded, and was arrested again in February 1998, according to The Age. A prosecutor told a 2022 bail hearing that Foster had a previous conviction for escaping custody in Victoria in 1998.

From a Brisbane police cell he sent a three-hour tape to Downing Street, the Independent reported. "I'm no angel," it said. The Guardian reported that while fighting extradition he claimed he would be killed in a British prison because he had helped expose a network of corrupt prison officers. His appeals failed. In September 2000 he pleaded guilty to three charges linked to Foremost Body, and was sentenced to 33 months. Because he had spent about 18 months in an Australian prison while fighting extradition, the Independent said, he was freed at once.

Foster's most public moment came in late 2002 through his then partner, Carole Caplin, the lifestyle adviser of Cherie Blair, wife of the prime minister Tony Blair. According to Crikey, Foster became an unofficial financial adviser to Mrs Blair and helped her buy two investment flats in Bristol on very favourable terms. The Independent said he allegedly helped her buy them while she was in Downing Street.

Downing Street first issued a statement denying that Mrs Blair knew Foster. Crikey reported that days later she made a tearful statement after an email from her to Foster was published, which read: "I cannot thank you enough for taking these negotiations over for me." NBC News wrote that the prime minister's media advisers stepped in and ordered a public apology. In the statement the Independent recalled, she declared that she was "not Superwoman". The affair was nicknamed "Cheriegate". Crikey wrote that Foster was deported from Britain in 2003 and afterwards said he knew more than he had told about Caplin and the Blairs.
content.h2: Fiji, Micronesia and the Vanuatu escape
content.p: After his release in 2000 Foster was in Fiji. The Age's writer met him on a cruise there in November 2000 and later reported that he was running a diet-pill business through a company called Chaste Corporation, and that in 2001 he gave $1 million to a new political party, "New Labour", and directed its campaign. That is the writer's account. Laisenia Qarase's SDL won that election.

In late 2006 he was arrested by Fijian authorities over fraud and immigration offences and held in a Suva hotel, The Age wrote. The Independent's account was that he tried to escape police by jumping into a river in his underpants. He skipped bail and fled to Vanuatu, where he was arrested on 14 January 2007. On 2 February the Port Vila Magistrates Court sentenced him to six weeks in jail, backdated to his arrest, and fined him 120,000 vatu (about A$1,400) for entering without a valid visa. He had pleaded guilty. The maximum was a fine of 200,000 vatu or 12 months in jail. Fiji police said that the extradition process was at an early stage, and the report said he faced three outstanding fraud charges there. The Independent said he reportedly talked his way out of prison there during a long lunch with his jailers.

The case that ended in a long sentence involved the Bank of the Federated States of Micronesia. Brisbane's court heard that Foster used false documents to obtain a loan of A$300,000 for a tourist resort in Fiji and used the money for other purposes, including credit card payments and his girlfriend's rent. In December 2007, after pleading guilty to money laundering, he was sentenced to four and a half years, with parole eligibility after half. RNZ reported that the loan was US$541,499, that he used US$286,408 to pay credit card debt and rent, and that a reparation order of US$199,794 was made. The Queensland Court of Appeal found the sentence was not excessive given his long history of dishonesty offences in many countries. Crikey reported on 1 May 2009 that he was being released that day from the Numinbah minimum security jail after two years and three months.

In September 2005 the Federal Court had banned Foster from the weight-loss industry. The Brisbane Times described that order as the one the competition regulator said he later breached. The regulator alleged that between December 2009 and September 2010 he was involved in marketing the diet spray SensaSlim, and that false claims were made about a worldwide clinical trial when none had been held. More than 100 people were believed to have paid A$60,000 for franchises. Giving evidence in September 2012, Foster said he had no involvement and had let a relative's boyfriend film a promotional video at the house he shared with his mother. "Only a moron," he said, would have done so if there were something to hide.

In October 2013 he was sentenced to three years' jail for contempt, The Guardian reported, and the allegation was that he had taken about A$6 million from 90 investors. He did not appear for the appeal hearing in Brisbane. He then said he was living in Fiji and sent a Sydney newspaper photographs of himself holding the country's main newspaper. Associated Press reported that police found him in scrub near Byron Bay on a Tuesday in October 2014 and that a scuffle followed. The next day, in a hospital gown, he pleaded guilty at Tweed Heads to assaulting police and resisting arrest. The magistrate imposed no extra sentence, and he went to prison to serve the earlier three-year term. The Guardian said his appeal had been thrown out in March, and that by October 2015 he was a year into an 18-month term. That month Justice John Logan released him six months early after Foster raised new, confidential circumstances. "I'm a very fortunate man," he said outside court.

In February 2017 Foster was extradited from Queensland to New South Wales over a sports-betting business, Sports Trading Club. The Canberra Times reported that he used the pseudonym Mark Hughes with an investor who spent more than A$1.3 million on an offshore betting licence, because an internet search would have revealed his name. He also had a false Irish passport in the name of Kevin Anthony McMullan, bearing his photograph, and other documents in the same name.

He pleaded guilty to making a false statement with intent to obtain a financial advantage, and to knowingly possessing the false passport. On 19 October 2018 Magistrate John Andrews noted a "lengthy criminal history, primarily in other jurisdictions". He backdated the sentence to when Foster entered custody, and the minimum term would have expired in July. Foster had spent one year, five months and 23 days on remand, and walked free. He arrived at court more than six hours late; his lawyer handed up a medical certificate saying he possibly had food poisoning and had missed his plane.
content.h2: Arrest at Port Douglas and the bitcoin charges
content.p: On 20 August 2020 Queensland police arrested Foster, then 57, on Four Mile Beach, Port Douglas, as he walked his dogs. The private investigation firm IFW Global said afterwards that its head, Ken Gamble, had helped New South Wales detectives look into a complaint about Sport Predictions, an Asia-based company the complainant called a sham front for Foster, and that Gamble had found him. ABC News noted that Gamble had also been hired by a media outlet to find Foster in 2014.

By May 2022 Foster had been charged in Queensland, accused of defrauding a Hong Kong pilot of bitcoin worth about A$2 million in 2019 and 2020. The counts were five of publishing false or misleading material, ten of dishonestly obtaining a financial advantage and one of dealing with proceeds of crime. Magistrate Janice Crawford granted bail on strict conditions: living with his sister, an ankle tracker, no travel beyond 50 kilometres. The prosecutor opposed bail. Foster's barrister said he had "dined out on his notoriety". The earlier New South Wales charges over the same matter had been withdrawn.

By November 2025, AAP reported, Foster, aged 63, faced five fraud counts of at least A$100,000 and one over A$30,000, plus charges of obtaining identification and producing false videos. He had not pleaded and told the court he was "adamant he has not committed any offence". His solicitor, Chris Hannay, said his activities for Sports Predictions Trading were legitimate. AAP reported that he had been awarded A$170,000 from New South Wales Police after a judge found in March that his 2020 arrest, filmed for the Nine Network's 60 Minutes, was not reasonable and proper. The case was adjourned to 24 February. He also said he was pursuing a television series based on an 800,000-word autobiography.
